analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and nursing homes to use mechanical lifts instead of manually lifting patients.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 46 House Democrats, was referred to three House committees and its subcommittees and never received a markup or floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Labor Department to write a workplace safety standard requiring hospitals, nursing homes, home health agencies, and similar facilities to use mechanical lifting devices instead of lifting and moving patients by hand, which is the leading cause of back injuries among nurses and aides. Employers would have had to write safety plans, buy and maintain lift equipment, train workers annually, and track injuries. Workers would gain the right to refuse unsafe lifting assignments, protection from retaliation for reporting violations, and the right to sue. The bill also authorized $200 million in grants to help facilities that could not afford the equipment.
analysis.who_benefits: Direct-care registered nurses, nursing aides, orderlies, and other health care workers who lift and move patients daily. The bill's own findings cite 24,340 musculoskeletal disorder cases among nursing aides in 2007, the second-highest of any occupation, and 8,580 among direct-care registered nurses, the seventh-highest [S3]. Patients also benefit, since the findings state mechanical lift programs reduce skin tears and the frequency of patients being dropped [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires health care employers to purchase, use, maintain, and have accessible an adequate number of safe lift mechanical devices within two years of a final standard, eliminating manual patient lifting except where patient care would be compromised [S3].

Gives workers the right to refuse an assignment that would violate the safety standard or for which they have not been trained, and bars employers from firing, demoting, or reporting them to state licensing boards for doing so [S3].

Bars retaliation against workers who in good faith report violations, participate in investigations, or discuss violations, and lets retaliated workers sue in federal court for reinstatement, lost pay, attorneys' fees, and other damages [S3].
Authorizes $200 million in grants to help health care facilities that demonstrate financial need purchase the required equipment, with $50 million set aside for home health agencies [S3].
Extends the standard even to facilities not covered by OSHA, through Medicare participation conditions under the Social Security Act [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, nursing homes, home health agencies, and other health care employers bear the cost of buying, maintaining, and training staff on mechanical lift equipment. The bill's findings note studies show such technology reduces workers' compensation costs and turnover over time [S3], but the up-front purchase costs fall on facilities, partially offset by the grant program.

drawbacks.text: The mandate imposes significant up-front equipment and compliance costs on health care facilities, especially financially strained nursing homes, rural clinics, and home health agencies, and the $200 million grant fund may cover only part of it [S3].

The bill requires eliminating manual lifting only 'to the greatest degree feasible,' so some manual lifting remains, and facilities must document every instance where equipment was not used, adding paperwork and administrative burden [S3].
Some facilities could face costs before equipment is fully in place, and the standard applies broadly to outpatient facilities, hospices, and clinics, not just hospitals [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a well-documented injury problem: its own findings cite tens of thousands of back-injury cases among nurses and aides annually and note that facilities that adopted lift equipment saw injuries, lost workdays, and workers' compensation costs fall [S3]. The main real cost is the equipment purchase for facilities, which the grant program partially offsets. The design is reasonably balanced—exemptions where patient care would be compromised, and money for facilities that cannot afford compliance.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to three House committees, then sent to two subcommittees, and none of them ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers, joined by Rep. Lynn Woolsey, introduced the bill on May 13, 2009 [S3].
It was referred to the Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means Committees on the day of introduction [S5].
Two days later it was referred to the Health Subcommittee and a month later to the Workforce Protections Subcommittee; the action history shows no markup, hearing, or floor action after that [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, nursing homes, and home health agencies avoided the equipment-purchase mandate and compliance costs, while nurses and aides continued working under the same lifting conditions.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 46 cosponsors was a House Democrat, and no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it; no chamber vote ever occurred [S4].

industries.industry: Hospitals, nursing homes, and home health agencies
industries.note: The bill would have required them to buy and maintain mechanical lift equipment, write safety plans, and face unscheduled inspections. Their interest in avoiding the mandate ran against the safety of the nurses and aides they employ and the patients they serve, though studies cited in the bill show lower injury and turnover costs over time.
A federal mandate for every health care facility to purchase and maintain mechanical lifting devices would have created a large, guaranteed market for this equipment.
